phy_edx.0.0.summary: Every physical quantity is a **number multiplied by a unit**, and Edexcel expects you to recall and use the **SI unit** for every quantity in the equations list, from the newton to the tesla. Large and small values are written using **prefixes** such as giga (G), mega (M), kilo (k), centi (c), milli (m), micro (μ) and nano (n), each of which is simply a power of ten. Getting units and prefixes right is worth marks on almost every calculation question in Papers 1 and 2, because a correct number with a wrong or missing unit often loses the final mark.

core.p: A **physical quantity** is anything that can be measured, such as mass, length, time or current. Every measurement has two parts: a **magnitude** (the number) and a **unit** (what the number counts). Writing 5 on its own means nothing; 5 m, 5 s and 5 kg are completely different things.
bullets: Quantity = number x unit, for example 3.2 m means 3.2 lots of one metre.
A unit is an agreed standard size so scientists everywhere get the same result.
In exams the unit is often a separate mark, so always write it after your final answer.
Symbols for quantities are written in italics in textbooks (m for mass), symbols for units are not (m for metre). The same letter can mean different things.

callouts.p: A property that can be measured and is expressed as a number multiplied by a unit.

core.h: The SI system and why it exists
core.p: SI stands for the **Systeme International d'Unites** (International System of Units). It is one agreed set of units used by scientists worldwide. Because every equation on the Edexcel equation sheet is written for SI units, you only get the right answer if you put SI units in.
bullets: Using one system avoids costly mistakes when teams use different units.
Equations such as E = m x c x delta T or P = I x V only work directly in SI units.
If values are given in non-SI units (g, km, minutes, kWh) you must usually convert them first.
SI units are built from a small set of **base units**; all other units are **derived** from them.

callouts.p: Convert every value into SI units BEFORE substituting into an equation, then the answer comes out in SI units too.

core.p: **Base units** are the fundamental units that everything else is built from. At GCSE you need the base units below; the most important ones are kilogram, metre, second, ampere and kelvin.
bullets: Mass: **kilogram (kg)**. Note the base unit of mass already contains a prefix (kilo).
Length: **metre (m)**.
Time: **second (s)**.
Electric current: **ampere (A)**, often shortened to amp.
Temperature: **kelvin (K)**. A temperature change of 1 K is the same size as a change of 1 degree C.
Amount of substance: mole (mol), used more in chemistry.

callouts.p: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram. Always convert grams to kilograms before using equations like KE = 1/2 x m x v^2.

core.p: A **derived unit** is made by combining base units, following the equation that defines the quantity. For example, speed = distance / time, so its unit is metres / seconds = m/s. Many derived units are given special names after scientists.
bullets: Speed and velocity: m/s (metres per second).
Acceleration: m/s^2 (velocity change per second, so m/s per s).
Force: **newton (N)**, where 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2 from F = m x a.
Energy and work: **joule (J)**, where 1 J = 1 N m from work done = F x d.
Power: **watt (W)**, where 1 W = 1 J/s.
Charge: **coulomb (C)**, where 1 C = 1 A s from Q = I x t.
Potential difference: **volt (V)**, where 1 V = 1 J/C.
Resistance: **ohm (Ω)**, where 1 Ω = 1 V/A.
Frequency: **hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz = 1 per second.
Pressure: **pascal (Pa)**, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2.

callouts.p: If you forget a unit, look at the equation: unit of the answer = units on the other side combined in the same way. Momentum = m x v, so its unit is kg m/s.

core.h: SI units for the Edexcel equations list
core.p: The specification requires you to **recall and use the SI unit** for every quantity on the equations list. These are the ones that come up most often across Papers 1 and 2.
bullets: Distance and displacement: metre (m).
Momentum: kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).
Weight: newton (N); gravitational field strength: newton per kilogram (N/kg).
Kinetic and gravitational potential energy: joule (J).
Efficiency: no unit (a ratio or percentage).
Wave speed: m/s; wavelength: m; frequency: Hz.
Density: kilogram per metre cubed (kg/m^3).
Specific heat capacity: J/kg degree C; specific latent heat: J/kg.
Spring constant: newton per metre (N/m).
Magnetic flux density: **tesla (T)**.
Moment of a force: newton metre (N m).

callouts.p: Units named after people use a capital letter for the symbol (N, J, W, Pa, Hz) but a lower-case letter when written in full (newton, joule, watt).

core.p: Physics deals with numbers that are enormous (the frequency of radio waves) and tiny (the wavelength of light). Writing 0.000 000 5 m every time is slow and easy to get wrong, so we put a **prefix** in front of the unit. A prefix is just a shorthand for **multiplying by a power of ten**.
bullets: **Multiples** make a unit bigger: kilo, mega, giga.
**Submultiples** make a unit smaller: centi, milli, micro, nano.
The prefix goes directly in front of the unit symbol with no space: km, MW, μA, nm.
A prefix does not change the quantity, only how it is written: 2 km and 2000 m are the same distance.

callouts.p: A letter placed in front of a unit to show that the unit is multiplied by a particular power of ten.

core.h: The seven prefixes you must know
core.p: Edexcel names these seven prefixes explicitly. Learn each one with its symbol, its power of ten and its value as an ordinary number. Notice that apart from centi they go up or down in steps of **1000 (10^3)**.

callouts.p: Capital M is mega (10^6) but lower-case m is milli (10^-3). A 5 MW turbine and a 5 mW laser differ by a factor of 1 000 000 000.

core.p: To change a prefixed value into the base unit, **multiply by the prefix value**. To change a base-unit value into a prefixed one, **divide by the prefix value**. A quick sense check: a bigger unit needs a smaller number, and a smaller unit needs a bigger number.
bullets: Prefixed to base unit: multiply. 4.5 kW = 4.5 x 1000 = 4500 W.
Base unit to prefixed: divide. 0.003 A = 0.003 / 0.001 = 3 mA.
Between two prefixes: go via the base unit. 2.5 MJ = 2 500 000 J = 2500 kJ.
Sense check: 1 km is a bigger unit than 1 m, so 3 km must be a bigger number of metres (3000).
When you see a prefix in an exam question, convert it straight away and write the SI value down.

callouts.p: Show the step, for example 250 g = 0.25 kg. If you then make an arithmetic slip, examiners can still award method marks.

core.h: Common non-SI units in exam questions
core.p: Exam questions often give data in everyday units to test whether you spot that a conversion is needed. You need to recognise these and know their SI equivalent.
bullets: Mass in grams (g): divide by 1000 to get kg.
Length in centimetres (cm) or millimetres (mm): divide by 100 or 1000 to get m.
Time in minutes or hours: multiply by 60 or 3600 to get s.
Energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh) on electricity bills: 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J.
Temperature in degrees Celsius: a change of 1 degree C equals a change of 1 K, so temperature differences need no conversion.
Speed in km/h: divide by 3.6 to get m/s.

callouts.p: 1 cm^3 is not 0.01 m^3. Because volume has three dimensions, 1 m^3 = 100 x 100 x 100 cm^3 = 1 000 000 cm^3.

core.h: Units in equations: checking with units
core.p: Units must balance on both sides of an equation, just like numbers. This lets you check whether a rearrangement is sensible and work out the unit of an unfamiliar quantity.
bullets: Example: P = E / t gives W = J / s, which matches the definition of the watt.
Example: V = I x R gives V = A x Ω, so Ω = V / A.
If your units do not match, you have probably rearranged the equation wrongly.
Some quantities have **no unit** because they are ratios of two quantities with the same unit, for example efficiency.

callouts.p: Whatever you do to the numbers in an equation, you do to the units. That is why kg x m/s^2 gives the newton.

core.p: When you write a final answer, choose a prefix that keeps the number between about 1 and 1000. This makes values easy to read and compare, and matches how data is presented in real Edexcel questions.
bullets: 0.000 45 A is clearer as 0.45 mA or 450 μA.
3 400 000 W is clearer as 3.4 MW.
Wavelengths of visible light are usually given in nm (about 400 nm to 700 nm).
Radio and mobile phone frequencies are often given in MHz and GHz.
Power station outputs are usually given in MW; household appliances in W or kW.

callouts.p: If a question says 'give your answer in kJ', you must use kJ. Leaving it in J loses the unit mark even if the number is otherwise right.

core.h: Prefixes and powers of ten on a calculator
core.p: Prefixes link directly to standard form. Using your calculator's x10^x (or EXP) button lets you type a prefixed value quickly and reduces slips with zeros.
bullets: To enter 5 μA, type 5 x10^x -6.
To enter 2.4 GHz, type 2.4 x10^x 9.
Do not type 'x 10' and then the x10^x key as well, or you will be out by a factor of 10.
Counting zeros by hand is the most common source of errors; using powers of ten avoids this.

callouts.p: Students often mix up micro (10^-6) with milli (10^-3) or nano (10^-9). The symbol μ is the Greek letter mu.

analogy.p: A prefix works like the difference between pennies and pounds: 250p and 2.50 pounds are exactly the same amount of money, just counted in different-sized units. In the same way 2500 m and 2.5 km are the same distance, and changing prefix never changes the actual quantity. The analogy breaks down because money only goes up in a factor of 100, while most SI prefixes go up in steps of 1000, and money has no equivalent of base and derived units.

terms.d: A measurable property expressed as a number multiplied by a unit.
An agreed standard amount of a quantity that measurements are compared against.
The International System of Units, the standard set of units used in science worldwide.
One of the fundamental SI units, such as the kilogram, metre, second, ampere and kelvin, from which other units are built.
A unit made by combining base units according to the equation for a quantity, for example m/s or the newton.
The SI unit of force; 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2.
The SI unit of energy and work done; 1 J is transferred when a force of 1 N moves through 1 m.
The SI unit of power, equal to 1 joule transferred per second.
The SI base unit of temperature; a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 degree C.
A symbol placed before a unit to multiply it by a power of ten.
A larger unit made with a prefix such as kilo, mega or giga.
A smaller unit made with a prefix such as centi, milli, micro or nano.
Prefix meaning x 10^9.
Prefix meaning x 10^6.
Prefix meaning x 10^-6.
Prefix meaning x 10^-9.

mistakes.w: The SI unit of mass is the gram.
mistakes.r: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

mistakes.w: Using a mass in grams directly in KE = 1/2 x m x v^2.
mistakes.r: Convert grams to kilograms first (divide by 1000).

mistakes.w: Writing MW when meaning mW, or the reverse.
mistakes.r: Capital M is mega (10^6); lower-case m is milli (10^-3).

mistakes.w: Leaving the final answer with no unit.
mistakes.r: Give the correct SI unit (or the unit asked for) with every final answer.

mistakes.w: Writing the unit of force as kg or the unit of weight as kg.
mistakes.r: Force and weight are measured in newtons (N); mass is in kg.
Power is measured in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.

mistakes.w: Writing 'Nm' for the unit of energy and 'J' for moment interchangeably without thinking.
mistakes.r: Use joules (J) for energy and newton metres (N m) for the moment of a force.
kilo means x 1000, so 5 km = 5000 m.

exam.q: State the SI unit of power.
exam.tip: One-word recall answers: give the name or the symbol, but spell it correctly.

exam.q: State the SI unit of electric charge.
exam.tip: Do not confuse with current (ampere).

exam.q: Which of these is the SI base unit of mass? A gram B kilogram C newton D tonne
exam.tip: The newton is the unit of force, so it is a distractor for mass.

exam.q: Write 0.000 006 A using a suitable prefix.
exam.tip: Count powers of ten: 0.000 006 = 6 x 10^-6, and 10^-6 is micro.

exam.q: A kettle has a power of 2.2 kW. Convert this to watts.
exam.tip: kilo means multiply by 1000.

exam.q: Light of wavelength 550 nm. Express this wavelength in metres.
exam.tip: Give the answer in standard form for very small numbers.

exam.q: Explain why the unit of momentum is kg m/s.
model: unit of mass (kg) multiplied by unit of velocity (m/s) gives kg m/s
exam.tip: Link the unit to the equation for the quantity.

exam.q: A ball of mass 150 g moves at 8.0 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
exam.tip: Using 150 instead of 0.15 gives 4800 J and loses marks.

exam.q: A power station has an output of 1.2 GW. A town uses 450 MW. Calculate how many such towns the station could supply.
model: converts to same unit: 1.2 GW = 1200 MW (or 450 MW = 0.45 GW)
exam.tip: Both values must be in the same unit before you divide.

exam.q: Explain why scientists use SI units and prefixes when recording and communicating measurements. Refer to examples in your answer.
model: SI units are an agreed international standard so everyone gets the same values
equations are written for SI units, so SI values can be substituted directly
prefixes are powers of ten that avoid writing many zeros (e.g. 3 GHz instead of 3 000 000 000 Hz)
this reduces errors and makes very large or small values easy to compare (e.g. nm for wavelength of light)
exam.tip: For a 4-mark explain question give four separate, linked points with examples.

worked.q: A phone charger supplies a current of 850 mA for 2 hours. Calculate the charge that flows. Use Q = I x t.
steps: Convert current to SI: 850 mA = 850 x 10^-3 A = 0.85 A
Convert time to SI: 2 hours = 2 x 3600 s = 7200 s

worked.q: A wind turbine generates 3.5 MW. Calculate the energy transferred in 1 minute, giving your answer in GJ.
steps: Convert to GJ: divide by 10^9, giving 0.21 GJ

worked.q: Work out the SI unit of pressure from the equation pressure = force / area, and show it is the same as the pascal.
steps: Unit of force is the newton (N)
Unit of area is the metre squared (m^2)
This combination is given the special name pascal (Pa), so 1 Pa = 1 N/m^2
worked.ans: N/m^2, which is called the pascal (Pa)

phy_edx.0.1.summary: Edexcel expects you to **convert between different units, including hours to seconds**, before using any equation, and to give answers to a sensible number of **significant figures** and in **standard form** where appropriate. Converting correctly means understanding whether to multiply or divide and remembering that squared and cubed units convert by squared and cubed factors. Significant figures and standard form show how precise a value is and make very large or very small numbers easy to write, compare and type into a calculator.

core.p: Every equation on the Edexcel equation sheet gives the right answer only when the values are in **SI units**. Questions deliberately give data in minutes, hours, grams, centimetres or kilowatt-hours to test whether you spot this. Converting first is the single biggest step in getting full marks on calculations.
bullets: Convert every value to SI units before substituting.
Write each conversion as a separate line so method marks can be given.
After calculating, convert the answer into any unit the question asks for.
Ask yourself: is my answer a sensible size? A car travelling at 3000 m/s means something has gone wrong.

callouts.p: Change all data into SI units (kg, m, s, A, J, W) before putting numbers into an equation.

core.p: The rule is simple: when changing to a **smaller unit** you get **more** of them, so **multiply**. When changing to a **bigger unit** you get **fewer** of them, so **divide**.
bullets: Big unit to small unit: multiply (3 km to m: x 1000 = 3000 m).
Small unit to big unit: divide (450 g to kg: / 1000 = 0.45 kg).
Always do a sense check: there are more seconds than minutes in any time interval.
Write the conversion factor down, for example 1 h = 3600 s, before using it.

callouts.p: If your converted number moved the wrong way (got smaller when the unit got smaller), you multiplied when you should have divided.

fig.cap: Changing to a smaller unit means more of them, so multiply; changing to a bigger unit means fewer of them, so divide. Time units are shown as the example.

core.h: Time conversions, including hours to seconds
core.p: The specification names **hours to seconds** specifically. Time is not decimal, so you must use factors of 60, not 100.
bullets: 1 minute = 60 s.
1 hour = 60 minutes = 60 x 60 = **3600 s**.
1 hour 15 minutes is 1.25 h, not 1.15 h, because 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour.
Half-lives and other long times may be given in days or years and may need converting in the same way.

callouts.p: 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes. Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60.

core.p: These conversion factors appear again and again in Edexcel papers. Learn them so you can apply them without thinking.
bullets: Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 tonne = 1000 kg.
Length: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 km = 1000 m.
Speed: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, so divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s.
Current: 1 A = 1000 mA.
Temperature differences: a change of 1 degree C equals a change of 1 K.

core.p: Some units are made from two units, such as km/h or g/cm^3. Convert **each part separately** and then combine them.
bullets: Quick rule for density: g/cm^3 x 1000 = kg/m^3.
Energy in kWh: power in kW x time in hours gives kWh; to get joules use watts and seconds.

callouts.p: km/h means kilometres per hour, so convert the top unit and the bottom unit, then divide one by the other.

core.p: Squared and cubed units convert by the **square or cube** of the length factor, because an area has two lengths multiplied together and a volume has three. This is the most common conversion trap.
bullets: 1 mm^2 = 10^-6 m^2, useful for wire cross-sections.
These conversions are needed for pressure (N/m^2) and density (kg/m^3) calculations.

callouts.p: Students often convert 50 cm^2 to 0.5 m^2. The correct answer is 50 / 10 000 = 0.005 m^2.

fig.cap: A 1 m cube has sides of 100 cm, so its volume is 100 x 100 x 100 = 1 000 000 cm^3. Its face has area 100 x 100 = 10 000 cm^2.

core.p: **Standard form** writes a number as **A x 10^n**, where A is at least 1 and less than 10, and n is a whole number. It is used for very large and very small numbers, which are common in physics.
bullets: Large numbers have a positive power: 3 000 000 = 3 x 10^6.
Small numbers have a negative power: 0.000 25 = 2.5 x 10^-4.
n tells you how many places the decimal point moves.
Speed of light: 3 x 10^8 m/s. Wavelength of green light: about 5 x 10^-7 m.
On a calculator use the x10^x (or EXP) button: 2.5 x10^x -4.

callouts.p: A number written as A x 10^n, where 1 is less than or equal to A, A is less than 10, and n is an integer.
45 x 10^5 is not in standard form because 45 is not between 1 and 10; it should be 4.5 x 10^6.

fig.cap: Converting to standard form: count how many places the decimal point moves to give a number between 1 and 10. Moving left gives a positive power, moving right gives a negative power.

core.p: When multiplying or dividing numbers in standard form, the calculator does most of the work, but you should understand the rules so you can spot errors.
bullets: Multiplying: multiply the A values and **add** the powers. (2 x 10^3) x (3 x 10^4) = 6 x 10^7.
Dividing: divide the A values and **subtract** the powers. (8 x 10^6) / (2 x 10^2) = 4 x 10^4.
If the result has A of 10 or more, adjust it: 12 x 10^5 = 1.2 x 10^6.
Use brackets on the calculator for divisions such as 6.0 x 10^5 / (2.0 x 10^-3).

callouts.p: If your calculator shows 4.5E-7 or 4.5 x 10^-7, write it as 4.5 x 10^-7. Never write '4.5E-7' as a final answer.

core.p: **Significant figures (s.f.)** are the digits in a number that carry meaning about its precision. The first significant figure is the first non-zero digit.
bullets: Non-zero digits are always significant: 352 has 3 s.f.
Zeros between non-zero digits are significant: 4023 has 4 s.f.
Leading zeros are not significant: 0.0062 has 2 s.f.
Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: 2.50 has 3 s.f.
Trailing zeros in a whole number may or may not be significant (3400 could be 2, 3 or 4 s.f.); standard form removes the doubt: 3.40 x 10^3 is 3 s.f.

callouts.p: The digits in a number, starting from the first non-zero digit, that show how precisely the value is known.

core.p: To round, count the required number of significant figures from the first non-zero digit, then look at the next digit: if it is 5 or more round up, otherwise leave it.
bullets: 3.847 to 2 s.f. = 3.8 (next digit 4, so round down).
48 760 to 3 s.f. = 48 800 (keep the zeros as place holders).
Do not round during a multi-step calculation; keep the full calculator value and round only the final answer.
Rounding too early can change the final digit and lose the accuracy mark.

callouts.p: Rounding 48 760 to 3 s.f. gives 48 800, not 488. Rounding must not change the size of the number.

core.h: How many significant figures to give
core.p: Your answer should be given to the **same number of significant figures as the least precise data** in the question (usually 2 or 3 s.f.). Giving too many digits suggests a precision that the measurements do not have.
bullets: If the data are given to 2 s.f. and 3 s.f., give your answer to 2 s.f. (or 3 s.f., which mark schemes usually accept).
If the question says 'give your answer to 2 significant figures', you must do exactly that.
Writing every calculator digit (for example 4.285714286) is not appropriate and may be penalised.
In practical work, the number of s.f. reflects the resolution of the measuring instrument.

callouts.p: An answer cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement used to calculate it.

core.p: A full-mark calculation follows the same pattern every time: convert, substitute, calculate, then present the answer with a suitable number of significant figures, standard form if the number is very large or small, and the correct unit.
bullets: Step 1: list the data and convert each value to SI units.
Step 2: choose and rearrange the equation if needed.
Step 3: substitute the SI values.
Step 4: calculate, keeping all digits.
Step 5: round to sensible s.f., use standard form where appropriate, and add the unit.

callouts.p: Mark schemes award marks for substitution and conversion even if the final answer is wrong, but only if the working is shown.

analogy.t: Significant figures are like the zoom on a photo
analogy.p: A measurement to 2 s.f. is like a blurry photo: you can see roughly what is there but not the fine detail. Quoting 8 s.f. from that blurry photo is like claiming to read a car number plate from a pixelated image; the extra digits are invented, not measured. The analogy breaks down because rounding follows exact rules (5 or more rounds up), whereas blurriness in a photo is not a simple step-by-step process.

terms.d: Changing a value from one unit into another without changing the actual quantity.
The number you multiply or divide by to change units, such as 3600 for hours to seconds.
The internationally agreed standard unit for a quantity, used in all equations.
A unit made from two or more units, such as m/s or kg/m^3.
A unit of energy equal to the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour, which is 3 600 000 J.
A way of writing a number as A x 10^n where A is at least 1 and less than 10 and n is an integer.
The index n in 10^n, showing how many places the decimal point has moved.
The digits in a number, counted from the first non-zero digit, that carry information about its precision.
Reducing the number of digits in a value while keeping it as close as possible to the original.
A zero that keeps the digits in the correct place value but is not necessarily significant.
How finely a value is specified, shown by the number of significant figures.
The smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can show.
The size of a number to the nearest power of ten.

mistakes.r: 2 hours = 2 x 3600 = 7200 s (120 is the number of minutes).

mistakes.w: Dividing km/h by 3600 to get m/s.
mistakes.r: Convert km to m (x 1000) and h to s (/ 3600), so overall divide by 3.6.
Round to a sensible number of significant figures, for example 4.3 W.
A must be between 1 and 10: 3.5 x 10^5.
Leading zeros are not significant, so 0.0042 has 2 s.f.
Keep place holders: 47 600 to 3 s.f. is 47 600; to 2 s.f. it is 48 000.

mistakes.w: Rounding at every step of a calculation.
mistakes.r: Keep full values in the calculator and only round the final answer.

exam.q: Convert 3 hours into seconds.
exam.tip: 1 hour = 3600 s.

exam.q: Write 0.000 072 m in standard form.
exam.tip: The decimal point moves 5 places to the right, so the power is -5.

exam.q: Give 0.045 68 to 2 significant figures.
exam.tip: Start counting from the first non-zero digit (4).

exam.q: A car travels at 54 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
exam.tip: Show both parts of the conversion for the method mark.

exam.q: A cyclist travels 18 km in 45 minutes. Calculate the average speed in m/s.
exam.tip: Convert both values to SI before dividing.

exam.q: A 2.0 kW heater is switched on for 1.5 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in joules. Give your answer in standard form.
exam.tip: Using minutes or kW directly gives the wrong number of joules.

exam.q: A block has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm^3. Calculate its density in kg/m^3.
exam.tip: Remember cm^3 to m^3 is x 10^-6, not x 10^-2.

exam.q: A student calculates a resistance as 23.076923 Ω using readings of 3.0 V and 0.13 A. Explain how the student should record this result.
model: so give answer to 2 s.f.: 23 Ω
exam.tip: Link the number of s.f. to the precision of the data.

exam.q: Light travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the time for light to travel 1.5 x 10^11 m from the Sun to the Earth.
exam.tip: Divide the A values and subtract the powers: 11 - 8 = 3.

exam.q: Describe how a student should process data given in mixed units (g, cm, minutes) to calculate a kinetic energy, and explain how the final answer should be presented.
model: convert mass from g to kg by dividing by 1000
convert distance from cm to m by dividing by 100
convert time from minutes to s by multiplying by 60
calculate speed = distance / time in m/s
calculate KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 using SI values, keeping full calculator values
give answer in J, rounded to the same s.f. as the least precise data, in standard form if very large or small
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence of steps with reasons.

worked.q: A train travels 126 km in 1 hour 24 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s, to 2 significant figures.
steps: Time: 1 h 24 min = 60 + 24 = 84 minutes = 84 x 60 = 5040 s

worked.q: An electric shower rated at 9.5 kW is used for 12 minutes each day. Calculate the energy transferred in one day, in joules and in kWh.
steps: In joules: P = 9500 W, t = 12 x 60 = 720 s

worked.q: A wire has a cross-sectional area of 0.50 mm^2. Convert this to m^2 in standard form.
